(1) Fructosamine and glycated albumin (GA) may complement plasma glucose and HbA1c in diabetes diagnosis and monitoring, which are biased by clinical and analytical factors — notably in patients with rapid glycemic changes, red blood cell disorders, or renal disease. Across clinical settings, GA's diagnostic efficiency and standardization exceed fructosamine's, with less sensitivity to preanalytical variables, lower reagent cost, and automation on conventional instruments; further studies must confirm whether GA can replace HbA1c. (2) WFS1, an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress regulator, is essential for glucose- and GLP-1-stimulated cAMP production and insulin biosynthesis/secretion. Glucose triggers WFS1 translocation from the ER to the plasma membrane, forming a complex with adenylyl cyclase 8 (AC8). ER stress and mutant WFS1 block this complex, reducing cAMP synthesis and insulin secretion, contributing to β-cell dysfunction and type 2 diabetes progression.

Two studies implicate mammalian RAD52 in break-induced replication (BIR) repair of collapsed DNA replication forks. A targeted siRNA screen for genes inhibiting G1-to-S progression under oncogenic cyclin E overexpression identified RAD52—dispensable for normal mouse development—as a top hit. In cells with oncogene- or chemical-induced fork collapse, Rad52 localized to DNA replication stress (DRS) foci; siRNA depletion or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout compromised fork restart and caused DNA damage. In cancer-prone heterozygous APC mutant mice, homozygous Rad52 deletion suppressed tumor growth and prolonged lifespan. Separately, mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) occurs at human telomeres, which resemble common fragile sites (CFSs). Telomeric MiDAS is widespread across cell lines regardless of telomerase- or ALT-based telomere maintenance, requires RAD52, and resembles CFS-associated MiDAS except it does not require the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease. Thus RAD52-dependent BIR helps cancer cells tolerate replication stress at collapsed forks and telomeres.

# Endosome-ER Contacts Control Actin Nucleation and Retromer Function through VAP-Dependent Regulation of PI4P

VAP (VAPA and VAPB) is an evolutionarily conserved endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-anchored protein that helps generate tethers between the ER and other membranes through which lipids are exchanged across adjacent bilayers. Here, we report that by regulating PI4P levels on endosomes, VAP affects WASH-dependent actin nucleation on these organelles and the function of the retromer, a protein coat responsible for endosome-to-Golgi traffic. VAP is recruited to retromer budding sites on endosomes via an interaction with the retromer SNX2 subunit. Cells lacking VAP accumulate high levels of PI4P, actin comets, and trans-Golgi proteins on endosomes. Such defects are mimicked by downregulation of OSBP, a VAP interactor and PI4P transporter that participates in VAP-dependent ER-endosomes tethers. These results reveal a role of PI4P in retromer-/WASH-dependent budding from endosomes. Collectively, our data show how the ER can control budding dynamics and association with the cytoskeleton of another membrane by direct contacts leading to bilayer lipid modifications.

Three papers. (1) FASEB J 2001 (10.1096/fj.00-0815fje): cholesterol is essential for synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration; ex vivo cholesterol efflux induced by human CSF-HDL3 and methyl-β-cyclodextrin impairs short- and long-term plasticity in adult rat hippocampal slices (CA1 fEPSPs). (2) ATM deficiency causes nuclear HDAC4 accumulation in neurons, driving ataxia-telangiectasia neurodegeneration; nuclear HDAC4 binds chromatin, MEF2A and CREB, altering gene expression. Blocking HDAC4 activity or nuclear accumulation rescues ATM-deficient mouse behaviors, though full rescue requires cytoplasmic HDAC4; ATM phosphorylation downregulates PP2A, excess activity of which dephosphorylates HDAC4. (3) Osteoblast-secreted PGE2 activates sensory-nerve EP4, inhibiting sympathetic activity via the CNS to regulate bone formation; PGE2 rises as bone density falls in osteoporotic models, and sensory nerve ablation erodes skeletal integrity.

Brown Norway rats with acute myeloid leukemia (induced by intraperitoneal injection of 10⁷ promyelocytic leukemia cells) were compared with healthy controls to test whether leukemia-associated oxidative stress evokes depression-like changes. Depression-like behavior was assessed via forced swim test at 30 or 34 days; spleen, cortex and hippocampus were excised. Leukemia altered locomotory and forced swim behavior in the 34-day series. Oxidative stress signs appeared at every stage: FRAP and glutathione were significantly lowered, while HO-1 mRNA and malondialdehyde were increased in spleen and brain. Glycine potency to displace [³H]L-689,560 from the NMDA receptor glycine site increased at 30 and 34 days; cortical 5-HT₂A receptors were upregulated at 30 days only. Conclusion: cortical antioxidant disturbances accompany NMDA glycine-site activation, characteristic of depression models, linking glutamatergic activity, oxidative stress and leukemia.

# Wolfram syndrome 1 and adenylyl cyclase 8 interact at the plasma membrane to regulate insulin production and secretion

Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress causes pancreatic β-cell dysfunction and contributes to β-cell loss and the progression of type 2 diabetes. Wolfram syndrome 1 (WFS1) has been shown to be an important regulator of the ER stress signalling pathway; however, its role in β-cell function remains unclear. Here we provide evidence that WFS1 is essential for glucose- and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-stimulated cyclic AMP production and regulation of insulin biosynthesis and secretion. Stimulation with glucose causes WFS1 translocation from the ER to the plasma membrane, where it forms a complex with adenylyl cyclase 8 (AC8), an essential cAMP-generating enzyme in the β-cell that integrates glucose and GLP-1 signalling. ER stress and mutant WFS1 inhibit complex formation and activation of AC8, reducing cAMP synthesis and insulin secretion. These findings reveal that an ER-stress-related protein has a distinct role outside the ER regulating both insulin biosynthesis and secretion. The reduction of WFS1 protein on the plasma membrane during ER stress is a contributing factor for β-cell dysfunction and progression of type 2 diabetes.

# Targeting BRCA1 and BRCA2 Deficiencies with G-Quadruplex-Interacting Compounds

G-quadruplex (G4)-forming genomic sequences, including telomeres, represent natural replication fork barriers. Stalled replication forks can be stabilized and restarted by homologous recombination (HR), which also repairs DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) arising at collapsed forks. We have previously shown that HR facilitates telomere replication. Here, we demonstrate that the replication efficiency of guanine-rich (G-rich) telomeric repeats is decreased significantly in cells lacking HR. Treatment with the G4-stabilizing compound pyridostatin (PDS) increases telomere fragility in BRCA2-deficient cells, suggesting that G4 formation drives telomere instability. Remarkably, PDS reduces proliferation of HR-defective cells by inducing DSB accumulation, checkpoint activation, and deregulated G2/M progression and by enhancing the replication defect intrinsic to HR deficiency. PDS toxicity extends to HR-defective cells that have acquired olaparib resistance through loss of 53BP1 or REV7. Altogether, these results highlight the therapeutic potential of G4-stabilizing drugs to selectively eliminate HR-compromised cells and tumors, including those resistant to PARP inhibition.

OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC first reprogrammed human somatic cells to pluripotency. Unlike in mouse, OCT4 substitution in human cells previously failed, but transcriptome/bioinformatic analysis identified lineage-specifier factors replacing OCT4 and SOX2 in human fibroblasts, supporting counteracting lineage-specification networks. HDAC inhibitor valproic acid boosted reprogramming efficiency over 100-fold (Oct4-GFP reporter) and enabled pluripotent stem cell induction without c-Myc. G-quadruplex (G4)-forming sequences, including telomeres, act as replication fork barriers; homologous recombination stabilizes/restarts stalled forks. G-rich telomeric repeat replication efficiency dropped significantly in HR-lacking cells, and G4-stabilizer pyridostatin increased telomere fragility in BRCA2-deficient cells, reducing proliferation via double-strand breaks, checkpoint activation, and deregulated G2/M—including olaparib-resistant cells (53BP1/REV7 loss). Psoralen-induced interstrand cross-links caused chromosome breakage and 4N delay only after S-phase; primary human fibroblasts removed ~2,500 ICLs/genome at ~11 ICLs/genome/h.

Loss of a glutamic acid in the AAA-ATPase torsinA causes most early-onset autosomal dominant primary dystonia. Snapin, which binds SNAP-25 and enhances SNARE–synaptotagmin association, interacts with wild-type and mutant torsinA, co-localizing with torsinA on PC12 dense core granules and in perinuclear inclusions containing DeltaE-torsinA in SH-SY5Y cells. FM1-43 and anti-synaptotagmin I assays showed wild-type torsinA overexpression inhibits synaptic vesicle endocytosis, while DeltaE-torsinA increases FM1-43 uptake; siRNA knockdown of snapin and/or torsinA similarly inhibited exo-endocytosis, and torsinA downregulation left synaptotagmin I on the plasma membrane. TorsinA thus acts with snapin in regulated exocytosis; DeltaE-torsinA acts by loss of function, possibly impairing dopamine uptake in dystonia. VAP (VAPA/VAPB), an ER-anchored tethering protein, regulates endosomal PI4P, affecting WASH-dependent actin nucleation and retromer function. VAP is recruited to retromer budding sites via SNX2; VAP-lacking cells accumulate PI4P, actin comets and trans-Golgi proteins on endosomes, mimicked by OSBP downregulation.
